issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: Parallel.ForAsync
comments:
> As for the motivation I think the same arguments for Parallel.ForEachAsync also applies to Parallel.ForAsync

Sort of.  With Parallel.ForEachAsync, the primary motivation was being able to consume `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, and once we're doing that, overloads that also support async bodies also make sense (and then once you have async bodies, you also want to consider `IEnumerable<T>`... it's a slippery slope).  With Parallel.For, `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` isn't a factor; the source is always synchronous since it's just a constant range.  There's still the possibility of an async body, but that's the minor aspect of the APIs.  There are also multiple ways to achieve the same basic functionality, e.g. the aforementioned layering on ForEachAsync, using Partitioner.Create to split up the range into individual iterators and spawning a task to process each partition, etc.

If we decide it's worthwhile to add Parallel.ForAsync, the proposed API set looks good to me.  I've marked it as ready for review to have a broader discussion about whether we want ForAsync at all.
Temporarily moving back to api-ready-for-review to discuss collapsing the int/long overloads to be just based on `T : notnull, IBinaryInteger<T>`

review_comments: ThrowIfNull takes object.  You can pass a T, but then if it's a value type at best it's a nop and at worst you're relying on the JIT eliding the boxing, which it will typically do but won't be able to all the time, e.g. in tier 0 since those optimizations are disabled.  Since this T will 99.999% of the time be a value type and I'm not concerned about this method being inlinable, I just wrote it out manually.

Should we consider creating an analyzer to suggest using the old null check + throw, instead of ThrowIfNull, for generic types?

I suspect the answer might be no, since you say 99.999% of the cases would be a value type.

No, I think we want to encourage using ThrowIfNull in general.  This is just a special case.

We could have an analyzer for ThrowIfNull with known value types (either an actual value type or a generic constrained to be a value type).  There's already an issue for that.
Do you think this delay be a good enough reason to move the test to outerloop? Here and elsewhere.
Yes.  Correctness doesn't depend on this delay, it just might not test as much as we want in some circumstances if things take longer than expected.
Oh, I misread the question.  No, I don't think this needs to be outerloop.  It's only 20 milliseconds.
Oh you're right. I was thinking in seconds.

Is this skipping to the next element if the next available element is not the same as the element + the next element?

I'm not sure I understand the purpose, or if I explained it correctly. Would you mind correcting me / explaining these lines?
It's incrementing by 1 in a thread-safe manner, as multiple threads could all be racing to increment at the same time.

For my own education, why is [CA1068](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/ba777a8ba43dde51bda84a13e0b251492fb9770a/eng/CodeAnalysis.src.globalconfig#L184-L185) not enforced in runtime APIs like this one?

This is mirroring what's done in the other overloads, where to better mimic what a loop looks like, the body delegate is last. The token is also in the same position as the options, which contains a token.

I'm curious: Does the `ThrowIfNull` method have a disadvantage when checking a generic argument?:

```cs
ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(fromInclusive, nameof(fromInclusive));
```

Not asking to change it. Just wanted to know if there are scenarios where the new method is preferred.
The 99.999% case here is these will be value types, in which case ThrowIfNull is at best a nop and at worst (if JIT optimizations don't kick in) a boxing allocation.
